query: Which bootstrap or subsampling schemes for dependent nonstationary data (blocked bootstrap, local bootstrap, dependent wild bootstrap) will we evaluate and how will we validate finite-sample calibration?

response.query: Which bootstrap or subsampling schemes for dependent nonstationary data (blocked bootstrap, local bootstrap, dependent wild bootstrap) will we evaluate and how will we validate finite-sample calibration?
response.answer: We will evaluate blocked bootstrap, local bootstrap, and dependent wild bootstrap. Validation of finite-sample calibration will use p-value calibration methods.

results.title: Bootstrap methods for dependent data | by Alex Heilman - Medium
results.content: Traditional bootstrap methods assume independent data samples, but in practice, data often exhibits dependencies, such as organizational hierarchy and time-series autocorrelation. In our software development domain, two common sources of dependence are: This article ultimately proposes an approach to account for these sources of dependence using the combination of two approaches: # **Independent data** This section provides an overview of how the bootstrap method is used to make inferences about the true population mean from a single sample using independent data. The distribution of these bootstrap statistics is used to form a 95 percent confidence interval, which estimates the uncertainty of the original sample mean. ## **The true population** Remember that we use the bootstrap method on *one sample* to make inferences about the *true population*. Note that the confidence interval captures the value of the true population mean shown in gray. ## **A frequentist’s intuition** We observed that the 95 percent confidence interval captured the true population mean. We were able to leverage one representative sample to construct a 95 percent confidence interval *without any knowledge of the population distribution*. This mean completion time aligns with the expected value of the population-generating function: With this population mean known to us, we are uniquely positioned to evaluate the accuracy of the bootstrap’s inference capabilities on dependent data. Ideally, we should see 95 percent of the bootstrap confidence intervals capture this true population mean of 20. ## **Standard bootstrap on dependent data** Given that we know the width of the population’s 95 percent tolerance interval, how would this compare to the standard bootstrap’s 95 percent confidence interval? In the figure below, we take one sample from the population, run the standard bootstrap for each month, and plot the resulting 95 percent confidence intervals. **Block bootstrap:** In an effort to preserve the temporally dependent structure of our data, suppose we created pseudo-samples by sampling all available data points in the block of time for each cluster. This result is exactly what we’d expect: 95 percent confidence intervals that capture the true population mean 95 percent of the time. Consequently, we achieved a 95 percent confidence interval that accurately captures the true population mean in 95 percent of iterations.
